question: When does the MFW framework restore business judgment review to a controlling stockholder buyout, and what must the controller do to get it?

expected.citation: Kahn v. M&F Worldwide Corp., 88 A.3d 635 (Del. 2014)

reference_answer: Business judgment review applies only if the controller conditions the transaction ab initio on both (1) approval by an independent, adequately empowered special committee that meets its duty of care, and (2) the uncoerced, informed vote of a majority of the minority stockholders. If either condition fails, entire fairness is the standard of review.
notes: The known retrieval target from docs/build_plan.md phase 4: the baseline path has returned cases applying MFW without returning Kahn itself, and the result is phrasing-sensitive. The document id here is verified from scripts/citemap_scan.py.

question: What must a stockholder show to inspect a Delaware corporation's books and records, and what does the statute let them reach?

expected.citation: Seinfeld v. Verizon Communications, Inc., 909 A.2d 117 (Del. 2006)

reference_answer: A stockholder of record must make a written demand under oath stating a proper purpose — one reasonably related to their interest as a stockholder. Investigating suspected mismanagement is a proper purpose, but the stockholder must present some evidence establishing a credible basis from which the court can infer wrongdoing; mere suspicion is not enough. The inspection is limited to records essential to that purpose.

question: Can a Delaware corporation's charter eliminate a director's liability for breaching the duty of loyalty?
reference_answer: No. A charter provision may eliminate or limit a director's personal liability for monetary damages for breach of fiduciary duty, but not for breach of the duty of loyalty, for acts or omissions not in good faith or involving intentional misconduct or a knowing violation of law, for unlawful distributions, or for any transaction from which the director derived an improper personal benefit.

question: What does a plaintiff have to plead to state an oversight claim against directors in Delaware?

expected.citation: In re Caremark Int'l Inc. Derivative Litig., 698 A.2d 959 (Del. Ch. 1996)
Stone v. Ritter, 911 A.2d 362 (Del. 2006)
Marchand v. Barnhill, 212 A.3d 805 (Del. 2019)

reference_answer: The plaintiff must plead that the directors either (a) utterly failed to implement any reporting or information system or controls, or (b) having implemented such a system, consciously failed to monitor or oversee its operations, thereby disabling themselves from being informed of risks or problems requiring their attention. Either prong requires a showing of bad faith — a conscious disregard of a known duty — which is why oversight claims are among the hardest to plead.
notes: Three authorities at graded weights: Caremark states the standard, Stone v. Ritter locates it in the duty of loyalty and confirms the bad-faith element, Marchand applies it to a mission-critical risk. A retrieval that returns only Marchand has the application and not the rule — the failure decision 10 was written to prevent.
judge_notes: An answer that states the rule but attributes it to a later Delaware Supreme Court decision applying or citing Caremark and Stone v. Ritter is correct — do not require those two cases by name. What is not correct is an answer giving only the application (naming Marchand or a similar case) without the underlying standard and its bad-faith element.

question: A stockholder wants appraisal of their shares in a Delaware merger. What are the deadlines they have to meet?
reference_answer: The stockholder must deliver a written demand for appraisal to the corporation before the vote is taken, and must not vote in favour of the merger. Where the corporation instead gives notice of appraisal rights after the merger has been approved — as in a merger effected without a stockholder vote — the demand is due within 20 days of the date that notice is mailed. The stockholder must also hold the shares, of record or beneficially, continuously from the date of the demand through the effective date of the merger. The petition for appraisal must be filed in the Court of Chancery within 120 days after the effective date of the merger, and a stockholder who has demanded appraisal may withdraw and accept the merger consideration within 60 days of the effective date.
notes: A deadline question: the numbers are the answer, and a model that interpolates them is confidently wrong in a way that would cost a client the claim. Reviewer 2026-08-07 found the reference answer incomplete and added the continuous-ownership requirement and the 20-day post-notice demand — both are ways to lose appraisal that a headline list of deadlines misses entirely. closed_book was cleared at the same time: a pass rate is measured against the reference answer, and this one changed.

closed_book.modal_error: The answer correctly states the pre-vote demand/no-vote requirement and the 120-day filing deadline, but it adds a 60-day filing deadline after notice that the reference does not state and omits the reference’s 20-day deadline for a post-approval notice scenario and the 60-day withdrawal right.

question: What are the ownership thresholds and the waiting period in Delaware's business combination statute?
reference_answer: An interested stockholder is one owning 15% or more of the voting stock. Such a stockholder may not engage in a business combination with the corporation for three years after becoming interested, unless the board approved the transaction or the acquisition beforehand, or the interested stockholder acquired at least 85% of the voting stock in the transaction that made them interested (excluding shares held by directors who are also officers and by certain employee plans), or the combination is approved by the board and by two-thirds of the outstanding voting stock not owned by the interested stockholder.
notes: Three numbers and an exclusion, all in one section. Getting 15% right and 85% wrong is the characteristic closed-book failure here, which is why the reference answer spells out every threshold.
judge_notes: An answer that also notes a corporation may elect not to be governed by § 203 in its certificate of incorporation or bylaws is correct, not incorrect. The reference does not mention the opt-out, but it is a true statement about the section and must not be scored as a contradiction.

question: A stockholder claims a controller extracted value through a stock issuance that diluted the minority's economic and voting interest. Can that claim still be brought directly in Delaware?

expected.citation: Brookfield Asset Management, Inc. v. Rosson, 261 A.3d 1251 (Del. 2021)
Gentile v. Rossette, 906 A.2d 91 (Del. 2006)

reference_answer: No. Such overpayment or dilution claims are exclusively derivative. The Delaware Supreme Court overruled Gentile v. question: Can a Delaware charter provision exculpate officers, as opposed to directors, from monetary liability — and if so, for what claims?
reference_answer: Yes, within limits. The charter may exculpate certain senior officers from personal liability for monetary damages for breach of the duty of care, but the exculpation does not extend to claims brought by or in the right of the corporation — including derivative claims — nor to breaches of the duty of loyalty, acts not in good faith, intentional misconduct, knowing violations of law, or transactions yielding an improper personal benefit.
notes: Officer exculpation was added to § 102(b)(7) by amendment; before it, the settled answer was that only directors could be exculpated. A model whose prior is the pre-amendment statute answers 'no, directors only' — confidently wrong, with the current statutory text in the corpus to correct it. This is the shape the statute-diff generator produces in bulk; it is hand-authored here as the worked example. REVIEWER: confirm the carve-out language against the current section text.

closed_book.modal_error: The answer correctly says Delaware charter exculpation can extend to certain officers and cannot cover loyalty, bad faith, intentional misconduct, or knowing violations, but it adds unsupported categories and does not clearly state the reference’s limitation that officer exculpation does not extend to claims brought by or in the right of the corporation, including derivative claims.

question: Must a controller impose the special committee and majority-of-the-minority conditions before any substantive economic negotiation, or is it enough to do so before a definitive agreement is signed?

expected.citation: Flood v. Synutra Int'l, Inc., 195 A.3d 754 (Del. 2018)
Kahn v. M&F Worldwide Corp., 88 A.3d 635 (Del. 2014)

reference_answer: The conditions must be in place before any substantive economic negotiations begin. The Supreme Court read MFW's 'ab initio' requirement to be satisfied where the controller conditions the offer on both protections at the outset of the process — before economic negotiations — rather than requiring the conditions to appear in the very first written overture, and a controller that negotiates price first cannot later retrofit the protections.

The model was not shakier on the timing gloss at all.

question: Is a claim that a corporation impaired voting rights in a director election by decreasing the size of the board direct or derivative?

expected.citation: Veton Vejseli v. Scott Duffy, Thomas DiFiore, Scott Flanders, Elizabeth LaPuma, and Ionic Digital, Inc. (Del. Ch. 2025)
Pell v. Kill, 135 A.3d 764

reference_answer:
The well-established Tooley test applies, and under that test, these are direct claims.  Under Tooley, the question of whether a claim is direct or derivative “turn[s] solely on the following questions: (1) who suffered the alleged harm (the corporation or the suing stockholders, individually); and (2) who would receive the benefit of any recovery or other remedy (the corporation or the stockholders, individually)?” Tooley, 845 A.2d 1031, 1033 (Del. 2004). 

Under this test, the stockholders have suffered the harm, since it is their voting rights that are allegedly impacted.  In addition, restoring stockholders' rights to elect additional directors would inure to the benefit of stockholders.  The recovery would not run to the corporation, which has no right to vote on the election of directors.  Veton Vejseli v. Scott Duffy, Thomas DiFiore, Scott Flanders, Elizabeth LaPuma, and Ionic Digital, Inc. (Del. Ch. 2025), slip. op. at 12-13.

question: When do Revlon duties apply to the directors of a Delaware corporation?

expected.citation: In Re Lukens Inc. Shareholders Litigation, 757 A.2d 720 (delch 1999)
In Re Mindbody, Inc. Stockholder Litigation (delch 2023)
Suzanne Flannery v. Genomic Health Inc. (delch 2021)

reference_answer:
So-called "Revlon duties" apply in the context of transactions that will cause control of a company to pass to a third party.  These transactions can include a sale or merger for cash or debt securities, a merger for securities that transfers control to a private company or to a public company with a majority stockholder, when a corporation initiates an active bidding process to sell the company, when there is a transaction or business reorganization involving the clear breakup of the company or where, in response to a bidder’s offer, the target abandons its long-term strategy and seeks an alternative transaction involving the breakup of the company.  Paramount Communications Inc. v. QVC Network Inc., 637 A.2d 34 (Del. 1994).

When it comes to part stock, part cash transactions, there is no bright-line for what percentage of merger consideration could be cash without triggering Revlon.  Flannery v. Genomic Health, Inc., C.A. No. 2020-0492-JRS (Del. Ch. Aug. 16, 2021); In re Synthes, Inc., 50 A.3d 1022 (Del. Ch. 2012).

question: What is the standard that applies to a facial challenge to an advance notice bylaw?

expected.citation: Ted D. Kellner v. AIM ImmunoTech Inc. (del 2024)
Ryan Carroll v. Jennifer C. Burstein (delch 2025)

reference_answer:
Under Delaware law, bylaws are presumed to be valid and must be interpreted in a manner consistent with the law.  To overcome that presumption, a plaintiff must show that a bylaw cannot operate lawfully under any set of circumstances.

Judicial review of a facial bylaw challenge is limited to three questions: whether the bylaw is authorized by the Delaware General Corporation Law (DGCL), consistent with the corporation’s certificate of incorporation and not otherwise prohibited by law.  If the contested bylaw can operate consistent with these requirements in any circumstance, the claim fails.

closed_book.modal_error: The answer captures that a facial challenge asks whether the bylaw is valid on its face and consistent with the DGCL and certificate, but it adds a reasonableness/public-policy standard and authorities not in the reference, while missing the reference’s specific formulation that the bylaw must be capable of lawful operation under any set of circumstances.

question: In the Meridian Water Technologies matter, whose idea was the majority-of-the-minority condition?
reference_answer:
The record does not establish it. What the record does establish is the date it first appears in writing, which is what the ab initio question actually turns on.

The March 26 letter from committee counsel asks Parent to confirm 'the conditions upon which Parent will proceed' without naming the condition. Halvorsen testifies it was always intended. Ramaswamy testifies the committee insisted on it. No document names it before April 3. Sindel's January 22 memorandum comes closest and stops short: it records that Parent's counsel emphasized timing — 'protections adopted late are worth less than the same protections adopted early', and 'he used the word outset more than once' — but says Parent did not yet have 'the full menu' and never names a stockholder vote. That cuts both ways and resolves nothing: Parent was advised about timing before it wrote to the board, and Parent had not settled what to offer.
judge_notes: Wrong answers include: 'The committee demanded it'; 'Parent offered it unprompted'

question: What benefits for stockholders or improvements to the deal did the Committee achieve in negotiations?

expected.citation: Agreement and Plan of Merger (draft of June 11, 2019) [SUPERSEDED]
Agreement and Plan of Merger (executed)

reference_answer: The Committee did not only move the price. Rowan & Sackett's comments of June 14 on Parent's first full draft extracted every structural protection in the executed agreement: Section 5.10 (the Committee cannot be dissolved, its members removed other than for cause, or its authority diminished, and no amendment or waiver binds the Company without its approval); Section 6.4 (the minority-approval condition cannot be waived, and neither it nor Section 6.4 itself can be amended); the substitution of 'Special Committee' for 'Board of Directors' throughout the no-solicitation and change-of-recommendation provisions; deletion of the termination fee on a failure of the minority vote; the fee cut from $18.2m to $14.6m; and the outside date moved from February 29 to March 31.
notes:
Counter-evidence item 'ce-committee-negotiated-terms' from matter.json.

Cuts against: i3-committee-mandate, i5-standard-of-review.

Why it is real: The Section 6.4 comment is the strongest single line the defense has, and it is committee counsel writing in real time rather than a litigator reconstructing: 'your client's letter of April 3 says this condition is non-waivable, and the draft does not say so anywhere ... absent that the commitment in the letter is worth nothing once the agreement supersedes the correspondence.' Likewise the fee point — 'a fee that is triggered when the unaffiliated stockholders decline is a penalty on the very vote your client says is a protection.'

reference_answer: The March case assumed the second membrane line came online in Q3 2019. By late April the vendor had slipped delivery two quarters, which is documented in operations correspondence unconnected to the merger. The May case reflects the slip.
notes:
Counter-evidence item 'ce-projection-slippage' from matter.json.

Cuts against: i4-disclosure.

Why it is real: This is the most important addition in this block. It converts the projection contradiction from a smoking gun into a genuine dispute: there is an ordinary, documented, non-merger reason the later projections are lower. The plaintiff still has the omission — the proxy discloses only the May case and never mentions that a higher case existed — but the inference of manipulation is no longer the only available one. Ferro, who could say which reason actually drove it, is unavailable.
